original_question: Does every polygon admit at least one periodic billiard orbit?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Problem 10: "Does every polygon have a periodic orbit?" This is the paper's official formulation of the existence question your draft is aiming at. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core universal existence problem almost verbatim: it asks whether every polygonal billiard table has at least one periodic billiard orbit, which is exactly the content of Problem 10. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))
missing_details: "Polygon" here means a planar Euclidean polygon used as a billiard table in the sense of Section 4, not merely a convex simple polygon. The paper explicitly allows nonconvex polygons, polygons that are not simply connected, and even barriers (obstacles without interior). ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))

The billiard dynamics is the standard specular reflection law from Section 1: the trajectory reflects off sides by equal angles, and the reflection rule is undefined at corners. The paper's convention is that an orbit stops if it reaches a corner. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))

So the desired periodic orbit is implicitly a nonsingular billiard trajectory: it must avoid corners as reflection points and return after finitely many reflections to the same position-direction state with which it started. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))

The quantifier is over all polygons in this Section 4 sense, not only rational polygons, acute triangles, obtuse triangles, or simple polygons. The nearby discussion lists these only as partial positive cases or subcases. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))

The problem is purely existential: it asks for at least one periodic orbit, with no extra requirement of stability, minimal period, parity of the number of segments, or membership in a periodic band. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))

No algebraic ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or asymptotic "for sufficiently large" clause is part of this problem; the hidden assumptions are geometric and dynamical instead. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))
refined_question: For every planar Euclidean polygonal billiard table P, in the broad sense of Section 4 (P need not be convex or simply connected and may include barriers), does the standard billiard in P always admit a nonsingular periodic orbit—that is, a trajectory obeying specular reflection at the sides, never hitting a corner, and returning after finitely many reflections to its initial position and direction? ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))
justification: The draft is closest to Problem 10, not to the later complexity conjectures or triangle-specific refinements. I sharpened it only by making explicit the ambient setting and the paper's conventions that are implicit in the terse official statement: Section 1 defines the billiard map and says corner hits terminate the trajectory, Section 4 enlarges "polygon" to include nonconvex/non-simply-connected tables and barriers, and Section 5.4 confirms that this exact universal existence problem remains open and is supported by partial results for obtuse triangles. ([users.math.uoc.gr](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~frantzikinakis/ErgodicUnder2024/ApplicationsBilliardsII.pdf?utm_source=openai))
